svg.title: Choose a model that matches the measured variation
svg.desc: On the left, three flower genotype categories from the specified pink-parent cross have relative model weights1,2,1; these are theoretical expectations. On the right, a smooth conceptual trait-frequency curve shows continuous measurements with labelled axes but no numeric scale or invented observations. Its shape is not claimed to be universal or enough to infer a gene count. Several loci, environment and measurement can influence continuous variation. The existing qualitative plant example has a shared genotype with different heights under different light; it calls for controlled comparisons, not rejection of inheritance. Heritability concerns variation in a defined population and conditions, not the fraction of an individual trait caused by genes.

g.text: Choose a model that matches the measured variation
A qualitative diagram separates model weights from a conceptual continuous distribution.
Two evidence types: categorical model and continuous measurement
Shape alone does not count genes.
Right curve is conceptual, not supplied numerical data or a universal normal distribution.
Several loci, conditions and measurement can contribute. Shared genotype can give different heights.
Compare controlled conditions; heritability is about population variation, not a percentage of one person.
